text: For \(a=1\) this is Theorem 6.6; let \(a\ge2\), \(\gamma_5(Q)=1\), and let \(x_s\) have order \(3^a\) modulo \(\gamma_2\). Since \(\Lambda^2(C_{3^a}\times C_3^{s-1})\) has exponent \(3\), the factors \(\gamma_2/\gamma_3\), \(\gamma_3/\gamma_4\), \(\gamma_4\) are still elementary abelian, so identities (i)–(iii) of the proof of Theorem 6.6 hold for all \(x\in Q\), and moreover \([x^{3^n},y]=[x,y]^{3^n}\) for \(n\ge2\). The class \(x_s^{3^a}\gamma_3\) does not depend on the choice of \(x_s\), so there are two cases. If \(x_s^{3^a}\notin\gamma_3\), Tahara's (B) forces \(3\mid u_{is}\), every term involving \(x_s^{3^a}\) vanishes by the identity above, and the proof of Theorem 6.6 goes through. If \(x_s^{3^a}\in\gamma_3\), the coefficients \(u_{is}\) are unrestricted. For \(a\ge3\) all new terms are \(3^a\)-th powers of elements of \(\gamma_3\) and vanish. For \(a=2\), (E) now gives \(\sum_i[x_i^3,r_i]=-\sum_iu_{is}[x_i,x_s]^9\), so the pairing \(\tfrac12\sum_i[x_i^3,r_i]\) cancels, formally, only half of the new term \(\sum_iu_{is}[x_i^9,x_s]\) of \(g\); the remainder is \(\tfrac12[r_s^3,x_s]\) with \(r_s=\prod_ix_i^{3u_{is}}\), and condition (E) for the row \(s\), which sees \(u_{is}\) through (B) with \(d(s)/d(i)=3\), gives \(r_s^3\in\gamma_4\). So \(g=1\) for every admissible family. (This step is not void: a computation finds groups of order \(3^{16}\) with \(x_s^9\in\gamma_3\) and \([x_i^9,x_s]\ne1\).) Here \(\alpha^{(ss)}=0\) is read off Tahara's generators of types (V), (VI) [Tah81, pp. 150–151].

text: For a \(p\)-group \(P\) of \(p\)-class \(c\) let \(P^*\) be its \(p\)-covering group, \(M\le Z(P^*)\) the multiplier (elementary abelian, \(P^*/M\cong P\)) and \(N=P_{c+1}(P^*)\le M\) the nucleus [OBr90]. The immediate descendants of step size \(1\) are the \(Q=P^*/U\), \(U<M\) of index \(p\) with \(N\not\le U\), and then \(\langle z\rangle=M/U\) is central of order \(p\) with \(Q/\langle z\rangle\cong P\).

Lemma (a filter on parents). If one of \(M\cap P^{*\prime\prime}\), \(M\cap M_5(P^*)\), \(N\) and, when \(P\) has class \(3\), \(\gamma_4(P^*)\), lies in \(\gamma_5(P^*)\), then no immediate descendant \(Q\) of step size \(1\) of \(P\) is of class \(4\) with \(z\in Q''\cap M_5(Q)\).
Proof. (The lemma is also formally verified, in a more general form, §4.)

\(\gamma_n\), derived subgroups and the Jennings subgroups \(M_n=\prod_{ip^j\ge n}\gamma_i^{p^j}\) pass to quotients: \(X(P^*/U)=X(P^*)U/U\). Class \(4\) needs \(\gamma_5(P^*)\le U\) (and \(\gamma_4(P^*)
ot\le U\) if \(P\) has class \(3\)); \(z\in Q''\) needs \(M\cap P^{*\prime\prime}

Theorem. Let \(p\) be odd and \(P\) a finite \(p\)-group of class \(3\) with \(|\gamma_2(P)/\gamma_3(P)|=p^2\) and \(|\gamma_3(P)|=p\). Then \(P^{*\prime\prime}=1\). In particular every immediate descendant of step size \(1\) of \(P\) is metabelian, and \(P\) is rejected by Lemma 6.9.
Proof. (The theorem is also formally verified, in a more general form, §4.)

\(P''\subseteq\gamma_4(P)=1\), so \(P^{*\prime\prime}\le M\), and as the subgroups \(U\) of index \(p\) in \(M\) intersect trivially it suffices to show \(Q''=1\) for \(Q=P^*/U\). Here \(\gamma_4(Q)\le\langle z\rangle\). If \(z\notin\gamma_2(Q)\), then \(\gamma_2(Q)\cong\gamma_2(P)\) is abelian. If \(z\in\gamma_2(Q)\setminus\gamma_4(Q)\), then \(\gamma_4(Q)=1\) and \(Q''\subseteq\gamma_4(Q)=1\). If \(z\in\gamma_4(Q)\), then \(Q\) has the same factors \(\gamma_2/\gamma_3\), \(\gamma_3/\gamma_4\) as \(P\), and Lemma 6.3 gives \(Q''\subseteq\gamma_5(Q)=1\). (Lemma 6.3 does not apply to \(P^*\) itself, whose lower central factors are larger.)

Remark. • For \(p=2\) the theorem fails, as a computation shows: SmallGroup\((64,138)\) has type \((3,2,1)\), while its \(2\)-covering group has order \(2^{13}\), class \(4\) and \(|P^{*\prime\prime}|=2\); likewise SmallGroup\((128,i)\), \(i=522,599,621,1755\), and \(12\) groups of order \(2^8\). • A computational check: the hypothesis holds for \(13\,315\) groups of order \(3^8\) and \(2\,754\) of order \(7^7\), and \(P^{*\prime\prime}=1\) in all of them. • The theorem does not say that such \(P\) are terminal. Of the \(7\,824\) groups of order \(3^8\), type \((5,2,1)\) and rank \(5\) (SmallGroup\((3^8,i)\), \(1\,387\,558\le i\le1\,395\,381\)), a computation finds that \(190\) have nucleus of order \(3\), e.g. SmallGroup\((81,9)\times3^{1+2}_+\times C_3\), and that all of their descendants are metabelian of type \((5,2,1,1)\). Theorem 6.12 below says exactly which groups of type \((d,2,1)\) with \(P/\gamma_2\) elementary abelian are nonterminal, and on this block it selects exactly the \(190\) (by computation). Its conditions (N1)–(N3) and (E) alone hold for the \(190\) and also for \(573\) terminal groups; the Jacobi condition (J) separates the two.

Theorem. Let \(p\) be odd and \(P\) a finite \(p\)-group of type \((d,2,1)\) with \(P/\gamma_2(P)\) elementary abelian, and write \([a,b]=a^{-1}b^{-1}ab\). Then \(P\) is nonterminal (it has an immediate descendant, equivalently its nucleus is nontrivial) if and only if (N1) \(|Z(P)\cap\gamma_2(P)|=p^2\), (N2) \(\gamma_2(P)\) is elementary abelian, (N3) \(P^p\le Z(P)\), and (N4) the linear system (E)+(J) below over \(\mathbb F_p\) has a solution with \(c=1\).

To state (N4), assume (N1)–(N3) and choose a generator \(w\) of \(\gamma_3(P)\), elements \(v\in Z(P)\cap\gamma_2(P)\setminus\gamma_3(P)\) and \(u\in\gamma_2(P)\setminus Z(P)\), and generators \(x_1,\dots,x_d\) of \(P\). Then \(\gamma_2(P)=\langle u\rangle\times\langle v\rangle\times\langle w\rangle\), \(x_i^p\in\langle v,w\rangle\), and \[[x_i,x_j]=u^{\omega_1(i,j)}v^{\omega_2(i,j)}w^{\omega_3(i,j)},\qquad x_i^p=v^{\alpha_i}w^{\beta_i},\qquad [u,x_i]=w^{f_i},\] with alternating \(\omega_r\) and \(f\ne0\). The unknowns are \(c,\mu_u,\mu_v\in\mathbb F_p\) and \(\eta,\sigma\in\mathbb F_p^d\); let \(\varepsilon_3=1\) and \(\varepsilon_p=0\) for \(p\ge5\): for all \(1\le i,j\le d\), including \(i=j\), \[\text{(E)}\qquad \alpha_j\eta_i+c\,\beta_jf_i+\mu_u\,\omega_1(i,j)+\mu_v\,\omega_2(i,j)+\varepsilon_p\,c\,f_j^2\,\omega_1(i,j)=0,\] and for all \(1\le i<j<k\le d\), with \((a,b,e)\) running over the cyclic shifts of \((i,j,k)\), \[\text{(J)}\qquad \textstyle\sum_{(a,b,e)}\bigl(\omega_1(a,b)\,\sigma_e+\omega_2(a,b)\,\eta_e+c\,\omega_3(a,b)\,f_e\bigr)=0.\]
Proof. (The theorem is also formally verified, with “nonterminal” in the form of Lemma C.1, see §4; Remark 6.13(1) reports a computational check.)

\(P\) has \(p\)-class \(3\), so it is nonterminal if and only if there is a group \(Q\) with a central subgroup \(\langle z\rangle\) of order \(p\), \(Q/\langle z\rangle\cong P\) and \(\gamma_4(Q)\ne1\). In such \(Q\) we have \(\gamma_4(Q)=\langle z\rangle\), \(\gamma_5(Q)=1\), \(Q''=1\) by Lemma 6.3, and \(\gamma_3(Q)\) of exponent \(p\); (N1)–(N3) follow. Write \(A=\gamma_2(Q)\) additively and \(D_xa=[a,x]\): the \(D_x\) commute on \(A\) and products of three of them vanish. Then the Hall–Witt identity becomes \([x,y,t]+[y,t,x]+[t,x,y]=0\) exactly, and its \(z\)-component on generators is (J). Comparing \((x_j^p)^{x_i}\) with \((x_j[x_j,x_i])^p\) gives (E). The unknowns are the exponents of \(z\) in \([v,x_i]=z^{\eta_i}\), \([u,x_i]=w^{f_i}z^{\sigma_i}\), \([w,x_i]=z^{cf_i}\), \(u^p=z^{\mu_u}\), \(v^p=z^{\mu_v}\). Conversely, a solution defines a pc-presentation on \(x_1,\dots,x_d,u,v,w,z\). Its consistency test words differ in the exponent of \(z\) by \(-J\), \(\pm E\) or \(0\), so it is consistent, and the group it defines has \(\gamma_4=\langle z\rangle\ne1\).

Remark. • A computational check. For the \(7\,824\) groups of Remark 6.11(3) and for all groups of order \(p^7\), type \((4,2,1)\) and rank \(4\) (i.e. with \(P/\gamma_2\) elementary) with \(p=3,5,7\) (\(932\), \(1\,460\), \(2\,232\) groups), the nucleus was computed in two ways: with ANUPQ, and with GAP's own \(p\)-quotient of \(F/[R,F]R^p\). The two agree, and \(N\ne1\) exactly for the groups satisfying (N1)–(N4): \(190\), \(102\), \(110\), \(118\) groups. For each of these, the pc-presentation of the proof built from the solution was checked to be consistent, with \(\gamma_4\ne1\), and to map onto \(P\); so for these groups sufficiency does not rest on the consistency test. Without the term \(c\,\omega_3f\) in (J) the criterion gives wrong answers both ways: on the block it accepts \(295\) terminal groups and rejects \(13\) nonterminal ones. Code: compute/magnus. • The system is linear and homogeneous in \((c,\eta,\sigma,\mu_u,\mu_v)\), so (N4) is the solvability of an inhomogeneous linear system. The term with \(\varepsilon_p\) is \(\binom p3[x_j,x_i,x_j,x_j]\), the only place where \(p=3\) differs from \(p\ge5\). Whether (N4) holds does not depend on the choices made, since it is equivalent to nonterminality. • The criterion assumes \(P/\gamma_2\) elementary abelian, i.e. \(d(P)=d\); this implies that \(P\) has \(p\)-class \(3\), but not conversely. It covers all groups of order \(3^8\), type \((5,2,1)\) and rank \(5\), i.e. all possible parents in Theorem 6.14, but not all groups of type \((5,2,1)\): for instance \(M\times(C_9\rtimes C_9)\), with \(M\) of maximal class and order \(81\) and \(C_9\rtimes C_9\) non-abelian, has order \(3^8\), type \((5,2,1)\) and rank \(4\). Groups of type \((d,2,1)\) with \(P/\gamma_2\) not elementary are not treated here.

Theorem (Computer-assisted). \(D_5(Q)=\gamma_5(Q)\) for every \(3\)-group \(Q\) of order at most \(3^9\). Hence \(D_5(G)/\gamma_5(G)\) has no \(3\)-torsion for every finite group \(G\) whose Sylow \(3\)-subgroup has order at most \(3^9\).

Proof. By Theorem 5.4(3) a counterexample \(Q\) of least order has order \(3^8\) or \(3^9\), and Lemma 6.2 applies to it; for order \(3^9\) we may use the result for order \(3^8\). The deduction for \(G\) is as in Theorem 5.4.

Order \(3^8\). Every group is in the SmallGroups library (package sglppow [VLE]). Of the \(1\,396\,077\) groups, \(904\) are non-metabelian of class \(4\); all have rank \(3\) (as they must, Proposition 6.5), \(|Z|=|Q''|=|\gamma_4|=3\) and \(Q/\gamma_2\cong C_3^3\), types \((3,2,2,1)\) (\(889\)) and \((3,3,1,1)\) (\(15\)), by a computation over the library. So Theorem 6.6 gives \(D_5=1\) for all of them. Independently, \(699\) of them have \(z\in Q''\cap M_5\), and for each the truncated Magnus algebra (\(121\) monomials, modulo \(3^{19}\), with the exactness certificate \(3^{18}\Delta\subseteq\Delta^5+3^{19}\)) gives \(z\notin D_5\).

Order \(3^9\). Let \(Q\) be a counterexample and \(P=Q/\langle zangle\), of order \(3^8\) and class \(3\) or \(4\). By Proposition 6.5(2), \(d(Q)\in\{3,4\}\); the case \(d(Q)=5\), type \((5,2,1,1)\), is excluded by hand (alternatively, by Theorem 6.10: all \(7\,824\) possible parents are rejected by Lemma 6.9, as a full run confirms). For \(d\in\{3,4\}\) we use computation: of the \(771\,597\) groups \(P\) of order \(3^8\), rank \(3\) or \(4\) and class \(3\) or \(4\), \(3\,986\) pass the filter of Lemma 6.9; ANUPQ lists their \(305\,583\) immediate descendants of step size \(1\); \(64\,362\) have class \(4\), \(Q''
e1\) and cyclic centre, and \(62\,245\) of these have \(z\in Q''\cap M_5\). For each of the \(62\,245\) the truncated Magnus algebra gives \(z
otin D_5\), exactly. The presentations given to it were checked independently with ANUPQ (order \(3^9\), class \(4\), \(z\) central of order \(3\) in \(Q''\cap M_5\)). The filter was validated against full expansion on a range and a random sample of \(1500\) parents, without loss of a candidate. The descendant step was repeated with an ANUPQ in which the defects found in an audit of the package are fixed (https://ispacex.github.io/gap/; two of them give wrong descendants for inputs not met here): for each of the \(3\,986\) parents the numbers of descendants, of groups of class \(4\) with \(Q''
e1\) and cyclic centre, and of candidates are the same, and the \(62\,245\) presentations are identical.
Cost and data. The order-\(3^9\) run took \(3\) h \(21\) min on \(4\) cores; the filter cut the time per parent from about \(350\) to \(27\) ms. Code: compute/magnus.

This is the algebra of Remark 6.4(2). Let \(M=M_1\oplus M_2\oplus M_3\oplus M_4\) over \(\mathbb F_3\) with bases \(M_1=\langle e,k_1,k_2\rangle\), \(M_2=\langle u_1,u_2,\rho\rangle\), \(M_3=\langle t\rangle\), \(M_4=\langle w\rangle\), and the alternating bracket whose nonzero values on pairs of basis elements are, up to antisymmetry, \[\begin{gathered}[e,k_1]=u_1,\quad[e,k_2]=u_2,\quad[k_1,k_2]=\rho,\\ [k_1,u_2]=t,\quad[k_2,u_1]=-t,\quad[e,\rho]=-t,\quad[e,t]=w,\quad[u_1,u_2]=w.\end{gathered}\] It is graded, generated by \(M_1\), of type \((3,3,1,1)\), and \([M_2,M_2]=M_4\ne0\).

Jacobi identity. This is also formally verified, with \([e,\rho]=2t\), which is the same over \(\mathbb F_3\) (§4). The Jacobiator \(J(x,y,z)=[[x,y],z]+[[y,z],x]+[[z,x],y]\) is alternating and trilinear and vanishes in degrees \(\ge5\), so it suffices to check triples of distinct basis elements of total degree \(3\) or \(4\). Degree \(3\): \(J(e,k_1,k_2)=[u_1,k_2]+[\rho,e]+[k_1,u_2]=t+t+t=0\), since \(3=0\) in \(\mathbb F_3\). Degree \(4\), triples \((x,y,z)\) with \(x,y\in M_1\), \(z\in M_2\): as \([k_i,t]=0\) and \([\rho,M_2]=0\), \(J(k_1,k_2,z)=[\rho,z]-[k_1,[k_2,z]]+[k_2,[k_1,z]]=0\) and \(J(e,k_i,z)=[u_i,z]-[e,[k_i,z]]+[k_i,[e,z]]=[u_i,z]-[e,[k_i,z]]\); the last two terms are both \(w\) for \((i,z)=(1,u_2)\), both \(-w\) for \((i,z)=(2,u_1)\), and both \(0\) otherwise. (A machine check of all triples agrees.)

In the notation of the proof of Lemma 6.3, \(\varphi(e)=1\), \(K=\langle k_1,k_2\rangle\), \(u_i=\alpha(e,k_i)\), and \(\alpha(k_1,k_2)=\rho\ne0\) spans the radical of \(\omega\): with \(\dim M_2=3\) the form \(\omega\) may be degenerate, and the step \(\alpha(K,K)=0\) of that proof fails. The Jacobi identity for \((e,k_1,k_2)\), which there gives \(2\,\omega(u_1,u_2)=0\), here reads \(2\,\omega(u_1,u_2)=\beta(e,\rho)\), both sides being \(-1\); with these constants it holds only because \(3t=0\). Taking \([e,\rho]=2t\) instead (the same over \(\mathbb F_3\)) gives such an algebra over \(\mathbb F_p\) for every odd \(p\): then \(J(e,k_1,k_2)=t-2t+t=0\) and both sides above equal \(2\), while the degree-\(4\) triples are unaffected as \([k_i,t]=0\). The Jacobi identity over any commutative ring, and the type and \([M_2,M_2]\ne0\) over any field, are also formally verified (§4); a machine check of all triples for \(p=3,5,7,11\) agrees.
We write out the case \(a=2\), \(x_s^9\in\gamma_3\), of the proof of Theorem 6.8, the only case in which the new terms do not vanish by themselves. The other cases are as in the sketch.

Setting. \(Q\) is a finite \(3\)-group of class \(\le4\), \(Q/\gamma_2\cong C_9\times C_3^{s-1}\) with \(s\ge2\), and \(\gamma_i=\gamma_i(Q)\). Then \(\gamma_3\) is abelian, \(\gamma_4\) is central, \([\gamma_2,\gamma_3]=1\), \([\gamma_2,\gamma_2]\subseteq\gamma_4\), and for \(x\in Q\) the maps \(c\mapsto[c,x]\) and \(c\mapsto[x,c]\) are homomorphisms \(\gamma_3\to\gamma_4\) trivial on \(\gamma_4\).

Identities. (a) \(\gamma_2/\gamma_3\), \(\gamma_3/\gamma_4\) and \(\gamma_4\) are elementary abelian. Indeed, for a basis \(\bar x_1,\dots,\bar x_s\) of \(Q/\gamma_2\) with \(\bar x_s\) of order \(9\), \(\gamma_2/\gamma_3\) is spanned by the \([x_i,x_j]\gamma_3\), \(i<j\), where \(i<s\) and \([x_i,x_j]^3\equiv[x_i^3,x_j]\equiv1\pmod{\gamma_3}\) as \(x_i^3\in\gamma_2\); the other two factors are spanned by the values of bilinear maps whose first argument lies in the previous factor. Hence the proofs of the identities of Theorem 6.6 apply: \(\pi\colon\gamma_2/\gamma_3\to\gamma_3/\gamma_4\), \(a\mapsto a^3\gamma_4\), is a homomorphism and \((ab)^3=a^3b^3\) for \(a,b\in\gamma_2\); and identity (iii) holds for all \(x\in Q\). Moreover, by the Hall–Petrescu formula \((xy)^3\equiv x^3y^3\pmod{\gamma_3}\), so \(x\mapsto x^3\gamma_3\) is a homomorphism \(P\) from \(\Omega=\{x\in Q:x^3\in\gamma_2\}\) to \(\gamma_2/\gamma_3\), trivial on \(\gamma_2\). (b) \([x^9,y]=[x,y]^9\) for all \(x,y\in Q\). Let \(c=[x,y]\). Since \([c,x]\in\gamma_3\) commutes with \(c\) and \([c,x,x]\) is central, \([x^3,y]=c^{x^2}c^xc=c^3f\) with \(f=[c,x]^3[c,x,x]\in\gamma_4\). Put \(Z=x^3\) and \(d=[Z,y]\in\gamma_2\). By (iii), \([d,Z]=[d,x]^3\in\gamma_4\) is central, so \([x^9,y]=[Z^3,y]=d^{Z^2}d^Zd=d^3[d,Z]^3=d^3=c^9f^3=c^9\).

Basis. Let \(W=\Omega/\gamma_2\cong\mathbb F_3^s\), \(\bar P\colon W\to\gamma_2/\gamma_3\) the map induced by \(P\), \(m=\operatorname{rk}\bar P\), and \(\bar z=x_s^3\gamma_2\in W\); then \(\bar P(\bar z)=x_s^9\gamma_3=0\). Choose \(x_1,\dots,x_{s-1}\in\Omega\) such that \(\bar P(\bar x_1),\dots,\bar P(\bar x_m)\) is a basis of \(\operatorname{im}\bar P\) and \(\bar x_{m+1},\dots,\bar x_{s-1},\bar z\) is a basis of \(\ker\bar P\). Then \(\bar x_1,\dots,\bar x_{s-1}\) are independent modulo \(\langle\bar x_s\rangle\cap W=\langle\bar z\rangle\), and \(3^{s-1}\cdot9=|Q/\gamma_2|\), so \(x_1,\dots,x_s\) is a basis of uniqueness of \(Q/\gamma_2\) with \(d(i)=3\) for \(i<s\) and \(d(s)=9\). Put \(Y_i=x_i^3\) for \(i\le m\); these are independent modulo \(\gamma_3\), and we take \(x_{2k}=Y_k\) for \(k\le m\), completed to a basis of \(\gamma_2/\gamma_3\), and all \(e(k)=f(l)=3\) by (a). Then \(b_{ik}=\delta_{ik}\) for \(i\le m\), \(b_{ik}=0\) for \(m<i\le s\) (as \(x_i^3\in\gamma_3\) for \(m<i<s\) and \(x_s^9\in\gamma_3\)), and \(\zeta:=x_s^9\gamma_4=\sum_lc_{sl}\bar x_{3l}\).

Tahara's conditions. By [Tah81, Thm. 6.1], \(D_5(Q)\) is generated by the elements \[g=\sum_{i<j}u_{ij}\tfrac{d(j)}{d(i)}[x_i^{d(i)},x_j]+\sum_{i,k}v_{ik}\sum_{l>k}b_{il}[x_{2l},x_{2k}]+\sum_{i\le j\le k}w_{ijk}[x_i^{d(i)},x_j,x_k]\] over the integer families satisfying (A)–(F) (signs as in the proof of Theorem 6.6). With the orders above we use: (A) \(w_{iii}=0\); (B) for \(i<s\), \(\sum_{i<h\le s}u_{ih}b_{hk}-\sum_{h<i}u_{hi}b_{hk}+3v_{ik}+3v'_{ik}=0\), and for \(i=s\), \(-3\sum_{h<s}u_{hs}b_{hk}+9v_{sk}+3v'_{sk}=0\); (C) \(3\mid u_{ij}\) for \(i<j<s\) (for \(j=s\) it is empty, modulo \(d(i)=3\): in the part of Tahara's (C) with \(\binom{d(i)}3\) and \(\binom{d(i)}2\) the \(u\)-term carries the factor \(d(s)/d(i)=3\) and \(\binom32=3\), and in the part with \(\binom{d(s)}3\) and \(\binom{d(s)}2\), \(3\) divides \(\binom93\) and \(\binom92\)); (D) and (F) exactly as in the proof of Theorem 6.6; and (E), modulo \(3\), \[\sum_kv'_{ik}d_{kl}\equiv\sum_{h>i}u_{ih}c_{hl}-\sum_{h<i}u_{hi}\tfrac{d(i)}{d(h)}\bigl(\alpha^{(hi)}_l+c_{hl}\bigr)-E^w_{il},\] where \(E^w_{il}\) is a sum of products of a coefficient \(w_{\cdots}\), \(w'_{\cdots}\) or \(w''_{\cdots}\) with distinguished index \(g\) and some \(\alpha^{(gh)}_l\), \(g\le h\); here \(\alpha^{(gg)}=0\), as read off Tahara's generators of types (V), (VI) [Tah81, pp. 150–151].

\(g=1\) for every admissible family. (1) As in steps (1), (2) of the proof of Theorem 6.6, (D) with \(b_{hk}=\delta_{hk}\) (\(k\le m\)) shows that \(3\) divides every \(w\)-coefficient whose distinguished index is \(\le m\). Hence the \(w\)-part of \(g\) vanishes (for \(i\le m\) by this, for \(m<i<s\) because \(x_i^3\in\gamma_3\), and for \(i=s\) only \(w_{sss}=0\) occurs), and \(E^w_{il}\equiv0\) (for \(g\le m\) by this, for \(m<g<s\) because \([x_g^3,x_h]\in\gamma_4\), and for \(g=s\) because then \(h=s\)). (2) The \(u\)-part. For \(i<j<s\), as in step (3) there, \(u_{ij}[x_i^3,x_j]=u'_{ij}[Y_i,Y_j]\) with \(u_{ij}=3u'_{ij}\), and this is \(1\) unless \(i,j\le m\). For \(j=s\) the term is \([x_i^3,x_s]^{3u_{is}}=[x_i^9,x_s]^{u_{is}}\), since \([x_i^3,x_s]^3=(c^3f)^3=c^9\) in the notation of (b); it is \(1\) for \(m<i<s\), where \(x_i^9\in\gamma_4\). (3) The \(v\)-part is \(\sum_{k<i\le m}v_{ik}[Y_i,Y_k]\). (4) For \(i\le m\), (B) and (F) give, as in step (5) there (the term \(u_{is}b_{sk}\) is \(0\)), \(v'_{ik}=-v_{ik}-U_{ik}\) for \(k\le m\) and \(v'_{ik}=-v_{ik}\) for \(k>m\), with \(U\) the skew matrix \(U_{ik}=u'_{ik}\) (\(i<k\)), and \(v_{kk}\equiv0\), \(v_{lk}\equiv-v_{kl}\) for \(k,l\le m\), \(v_{kl}\equiv0\) for \(k\le m<l\). For \(i=s\), (B) gives \(v'_{sk}=u_{ks}-3v_{sk}\) for \(k\le m\) and \(v'_{sk}=-3v_{sk}\) for \(k>m\). (5) Put \(a_i=\prod_kx_{2k}^{v'_{ik}}\in\gamma_2\), so that the left side of (E) is the coordinate vector of \(\pi(a_i\gamma_3)\). For \(i\le m\) the terms with \(h<i\) vanish modulo \(3\) by (C), and of those with \(h>i\) only \(h=s\) survives; so \(\pi(a_i)=u_{is}\zeta\). For \(i=s\) every \(u\)-term carries the factor \(d(s)/d(h)=3\), so \(\pi(a_s)=0\). Let \(M=v+U\) on indices \(\le m\) (skew with zero diagonal modulo \(3\)), \(r_i=\prod_{k\le m}Y_k^{M_{ik}}\) for \(i\le m\), and \(r_s=\prod_{i\le m}Y_i^{u_{is}}\). By (4), \(a_i\equiv r_i^{-1}\) and \(a_s\equiv r_s\pmod{\gamma_3}\); therefore \[r_i^3\equiv x_s^{-9u_{is}}\pmod{\gamma_4}\quad(i\le m),\qquad r_s^3\in\gamma_4.\] (6) Writing \(\gamma_4\) additively (exponent \(3\), so \(\tfrac12\) makes sense), \[g=\sum_{k<i\le m}M_{ik}[Y_i,Y_k]+\sum_{i\le m}u_{is}[x_i^9,x_s]=\tfrac12\sum_{i\le m}[Y_i,r_i]+\sum_{i\le m}u_{is}[x_i^9,x_s].\] By identity (iii) and (5), \([Y_i,r_i]=[x_i^3,r_i]=[x_i,r_i^3]=[x_i,x_s^9]^{-u_{is}}\), and by (b), \([x_i,x_s^9]=[x_s,x_i]^{-9}=[x_i,x_s]^9=[x_i^9,x_s]\). So, formally, the pairing cancels only half of the new term (in \(\gamma_4\), of exponent \(3\), \(\tfrac12=-1\)): \[g=\bigl(1-\tfrac12\bigr)\sum_{i\le m}u_{is}[x_i^9,x_s]=\tfrac12\Bigl[\prod_{i\le m}x_i^{9u_{is}},\,x_s\Bigr]=\tfrac12\,[r_s^3,x_s],\] since \(x_i^9=Y_i^3\in\gamma_3\) and \(\prod_iY_i^{3u_{is}}=r_s^3\) by (a). By (5), \(r_s^3\in\gamma_4\) is central, so \(g=1\).

The last step is where the row \(s\) of (E) is needed: it sees \(u_{is}\) through \(v'_{sk}\) in (B), where \(d(s)/d(i)=3\). The terms \([x_i^9,x_s]\) need not vanish (see the sketch). The whole computation is also part of the Lean proof of Theorem 6.8 (ExpThreePlus.lean, Setup8.gen_eq_one).

Throughout, \(p\) is odd, \(P\) is as in Theorem 6.12, \(V=P/\gamma_2(P)\cong\mathbb F_p^d\), \([a,b]=a^{-1}b^{-1}ab\), \([a,b,c]=[[a,b],c]\), and \(P_i\) is the lower exponent-\(p\) central series. Steps 2, 4 and 5 are also formally verified (Step 5 with a different construction of \(Q\), up to the final appeal to Lemma C.1), see §4.
